items.content_excerpt: A chart is one JSON spec. validate() and repair() check and fix it locally, with no model call and no hosted service. The same spec draws as SVG in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Qwik, Angular, Astro, plain DOM, or Node. svg is a string. It needs no browser, so the same call works in Node, in a build step, or in an edge worker. A line chart is 32 KB gzip. uPlot is smaller at 24 KB. We publish the benchmarks we lose as well as the ones we win: BENCHMARKS.md . Nothing to install: ChartKit Cloud does the same render over HTTP. Send a spec to /render and get an SVG or PNG back. Agents can call its remote MCP, which has three tools: render_chart , validate_chart and repair_chart . It goes live at cloud.chartkit.dev with v1. The service is in apps/cloud . The chart is static SVG with no client script. The build fails on an invalid spec. Add the client prop for tooltips and selection. Each of these also prints the SVG during server rendering. Their READMEs are in packages/ . By default an adapter can draw every chart type. To ship one type, pass render from createRenderer([...]) . validate() returns coded diagnostics ( CK1003 and so on), and each one carries a JSON Patch fix where a fix is safe. repair() applies those fixes. Both are deterministic and run in your process. repairAsync() from @chartkitdev/core/validate/convert also converts Chart.js, ECharts, Plotly, Vega-Lite and Recharts configs. items.title: Show HN: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB
items.summary: Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents. That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months. It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup. I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees. The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them. This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far) I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups. - Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

items.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
items.summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

items.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
items.summary: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache. Once lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch at the entry boundary, deep cached context substitutes for skipped token-local passes, allowing late entry to outperform matched early exit across model families and pass budgets. To turn this asymmetry into wall-clock speedups without stalling to build deep caches, candidate blocks verify through only the final K passes on the critical path while previously committed tokens complete passes 1 -> T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.

items.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
items.summary: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

items.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. items.title: claude-code v2.1.326
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while agent teams are enabled; if you already turned it on, sessions with teams on now start in Code Mode
  • Added a startup warning when an --allowedTools, --disallowedTools or --tools value has an entry that doesn't look like a complete rule
  • Added a message explaining why MCP servers stop loading when an administrator adds managed-mcp.json during a session
  • Added a row to /status that says when your provider or an environment variable such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY turns features off
  • Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin list when a malformed plugin.json field such as author or homepage is ignored
  • Added Ctrl+O to show hidden startup notices
  • Added a hint in the empty prompt that says what to do after a request fails
  • Added an esc to stop footer hint in a subagent's view where Esc would stop it
  • Added OTEL_RESOURCE_INCLUDE_HOST to include host.name and host.id in OpenTelemetry resource attributes (off by default)
  • Added overflowX="scroll" on a mod's Box, and maxLines and wrap="clip" on its Text
  • Fixed cp of a file being refused when only its source was covered by an Edit deny rule
  • Fixed Bash commands that delete or overwrite files (find -delete, cat a > b, sort -o) being summed up in the transcript as a search or a read
  • Fixed a misleading "Dangerous rm operation" warning in the Bash permission prompt on some commands with no rm that Claude Code can't read reliably
  • Fixed background sessions losing the LLM gateway your shell exported after a crash, after a reopen from another folder, or when the background service lacks it: they now stop before any model request
  • Fixed the background service ending your own processes, such as an SSH login, when a process number on its list had been reused by another user's process
  • Fixed rules added in /permissions or at a main-conversation tool prompt, and /add-dir folders, looking saved when the settings file couldn't be written; the terminal now warns and names it
  • Fixed a failed MCP headersHelper, or one not run in an untrusted folder, making other sessions start without that server, for most servers with no stored OAuth refresh token
  • Fixed managed settings with certain key names stopping Claude Code from starting or affecting other managed files
  • Fixed settings files with values nested thousands of levels deep crashing Claude Code or applying only some of the time; values past 64 levels are now dropped with a warning
  • Fixed a settings file saved with an error mid-session being skipped silently; a warning now names the file
  • Fixed the subagent model set in managed settings not applying in Claude Desktop's Code tab; it now overrides your own, as in a terminal, unless those settings also pick a provider or gateway
  • Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when the home or config directory is reached through a symlink into /net and sandbox settings deny reads of it
  • Fixed empty placeholder files, including .git/config.lock, sometimes being left in the project on Linux when Claude Code was stopped during a sandboxed command
  • Fixed Up then Enter answering Yes at the folder trust prompt shown under an already trusted parent folder
  • Fixed an extra Enter at the end of setup accepting the offer to make auto mode the default
  • Fixed a message typed over the startup auto mode offer being lost, and its Enter accepting the offer
  • Fixed a note typed on a permission prompt being sent to Claude after Tab had hidden it
  • Fixed PreToolUse hooks in managed settings leaving no OpenTelemetry tool_decision event or permission_denials entry when they refused a direct tool call
  • Fixed letters typed over /sandbox or a delete question in /permissions moving the selection
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing recent turns after a crash when the previous turn ended with an empty reply
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing earlier conversation history when Claude Code ran low on memory
  • Fixed a re-sent file overwriting Claude's changed copy in Remote Control and cloud sessions on Linux with no feature flags loaded: the copy moves to a .kept- folder, or the new file isn't saved
  • Fixed a background session being killed and its request lost when you opened, stopped or removed the older session whose conversation it had resumed
  • Fixed claude purge hiding its prompts when stdout is redirected, where one unseen Enter could delete a project's data; they now show on the terminal
  • Fixed the spend limit menu removing the monthly limit without asking when Backspace and Enter were pressed as it opened
  • Fixed /rewind restoring only some files after running /branch twice while a slow backup copy was still running
  • Fixed /rewind saying "No code changes" when a shell command changed files it can't restore; a turn whose changes weren't tracked now reads "Code changes unknown"
  • Fixed /rewind: Esc now cancels its summary, its list shows more than one past prompt in fullscreen, and a long prompt no longer hides its warning about losing later file changes
  • Fixed Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D twice in /skills quitting Claude Code and dropping changes; it now saves and closes the panel
  • Fixed the usage limit menu erasing your draft and opening while you were typing
  • Fixed pasted text and images being dropped when ↑ recalls a draft cleared with Esc Esc
  • Fixed an edited typed answer to Claude's question sending the old text when you moved on without pressing Enter
  • Fixed going back to a question you answered from its list putting the cursor on the first option, where Enter replaced your answer
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug sending the report when you typed a space on the confirmation screen, and losing the typed report after Ctrl+O or Ctrl+Z
  • Fixed a prompt typed after --add-dir, --allowedTools or another list option being dropped without a message

  • Fixed an error when max_tokens exceeded the model's limit: Claude Code now retries the request with the maximum the Anthropic API reports
  • Fixed grep in the Bash tool silently skipping some text files
  • Fixed a crashed Node or Python hook showing only the first line of its stack trace; the error is now shown, and Ctrl+O shows up to 10,000 characters of the output

  • Fixed pressing c to copy an MCP sign-in URL leaving a stray c in the paste field
  • Fixed Tab and Shift+Tab not moving between fields in an MCP server's input form, and a required field there keeping its tick after being emptied
  • Remote Control: Fixed a session disconnecting mid-reply when the server was briefly unavailable
  • Remote Control: Fixed the QR code in /remote-control being cut off in short terminal windows such as 80×24

  • Fixed /teleport hiding a session from its list in narrow terminals
  • Fixed artifact publishing refusing files in a background session's temporary folder
  • Fixed subagents whose disallowedTools lists Artifact still being offered artifact tools in some cloud sessions

  • Fixed the "background agents launched" line stopping at two when Claude starts three or more agents in one reply

  • Fixed some very long Bash or PowerShell commands freezing the session for seconds
  • Fixed Shift+Enter or Option+Enter pressed right after a paste sending the prompt instead of adding a new line
  • Fixed Up, Down, End and mouse clicks putting the cursor on the wrong row of a prompt that wraps
  • Fixed undo (Ctrl+_) losing the last words typed when pressed after deleting a line or word
  • Fixed code or a diff pasted into a prompt losing its indentation in the transcript, and a pasted diff's added lines showing as removed
  • Fixed [Image #N] landing in the middle of a word when typing right after pasting, and a pasted image not being sent after deleting its placeholder and pasting it back with Ctrl+Y
  • Fixed asterisks disappearing from your own prompts in the transcript, such as src/**/*.ts or 2*3*4
  • Fixed claude -p showing nothing in the terminal while it retried an overloaded or failing API request, or when it failed with its text output redirected or captured
  • Fixed Windows paths in Claude's responses losing the backslash before folders like .claude or _build
  • Fixed bold text showing as raw ** in Japanese, Chinese and Korean replies when it starts or ends with punctuation
  • Fixed /memory opening a read-only file with no warning that changes may not save
  • Fixed Claude editing ~/.claude/keybindings.json, which has no effect in Claude Desktop, when asked to change a shortcut there
  • Fixed Claude saying that an administrator can turn on Claude in Chrome when your organization's policy disables it, in apps that provide its tools such as Claude Desktop's Code tab
  • Fixed the suggested next prompt sometimes being a bare tag, such as <signal type="empty" />
  • Fixed long command output ending mid-line in the expanded view with no sign it was cut; it now names the saved file
  • Fixed collapsed tool lines reading "Ran" or "Called" while still asking permission, and "Running…" or "Reading…" again when a panel opened after a call was stopped or refused
  • Fixed failed, blocked or refused commands looking like passing ones in a collapsed tool line: it now shows "· 1 failed" or says they did not run
  • Fixed the "done" line showing after a turn that failed or was refused at a permission prompt
  • Fixed failed or refused skill and agent calls still showing "Initializing…"

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
